items.stem: (a) Describe the effects of the First World War on Russia. [4] (b) Why did the First World War weaken the Tsar's rule? [6]
items.answer: (a) Heavy defeats, such as Tannenberg in 1914, and millions of casualties. Shortages of weapons, boots and supplies for the army. Food and fuel shortages in the cities as the railways were overwhelmed. Prices rose rapidly. The Tsar was blamed after he took command in 1915. Rasputin's influence over the Tsarina damaged the royal family's reputation. (b) Defeats and huge casualties destroyed confidence in the government. Taking command made Nicholas personally responsible. Shortages of food and fuel caused hardship and strikes in the cities. The influence of Rasputin and the German-born Tsarina discredited the monarchy. The army, the Tsar's main support, became unreliable.

items.stem: In March 1917 (February in the old Russian calendar) Nicholas II abdicated. Describe the events of the February Revolution of 1917.
items.answer: Strikes and bread riots broke out in Petrograd. Women marched on International Women's Day. Soldiers refused to fire on the crowds and joined them. The Duma set up a Provisional Committee and the Petrograd Soviet was formed. Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917.

items.stem: ‘The First World War was the main reason for the collapse of tsarism in 1917.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Defeats and casualties discredited the regime. Shortages caused the bread riots and strikes of February 1917. The army, demoralised by the war, refused to defend the Tsar. Against: Long-term problems: poverty of peasants and workers, demands for reform since 1905. Nicholas II's weak leadership and refusal to share power. The influence of Rasputin and the Tsarina. The Tsar had survived 1905 only by making promises he later took back. Judgement: The war turned long-term discontent into revolution, but the Tsar's own failings and the weaknesses of autocracy explain why the war proved fatal.

items.stem: From March to October 1917 Russia was ruled by the Provisional Government. (a) Describe the problems faced by the Provisional Government in 1917. [4] (b) Why did the Provisional Government become unpopular? [6]
items.answer: (a) It shared power with the Petrograd Soviet, whose Order No. 1 controlled the soldiers. It continued the war, which was very unpopular. It delayed land reform until a Constituent Assembly met. Food shortages and inflation continued. It faced challenges from the left (July Days) and the right (Kornilov). (b) It kept Russia in the war, and the June offensive of 1917 failed. It did not give land to the peasants. It failed to solve shortages of food and fuel. It had to share power with the Soviet. Kerensky's handling of the Kornilov affair made him look weak.

items.stem: From March to October 1917 Russia was ruled by the Provisional Government. ‘The weakness of the Provisional Government was the main reason why the Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It stayed in the war and failed to give land or solve food shortages. It shared power with the Soviet. The Kornilov affair left it without military support. Against: Lenin's leadership and slogans won support. Trotsky's organisation of the Red Guards made the takeover possible. The Bolsheviks were disciplined and determined. Bolsheviks controlled the Petrograd Soviet by September 1917. Judgement: The Provisional Government's weakness created the opportunity, but Lenin and Trotsky's leadership explain why the Bolsheviks, rather than another group, took it.

items.stem: Describe the New Economic Policy.
items.answer: Requisitioning was replaced by a tax in kind. Peasants could sell surplus grain for profit. Small businesses could be privately owned. Large industries, banks and foreign trade stayed under state control. Nepmen traders appeared and production recovered.

items.stem: (a) Describe War Communism. [4] (b) Why did Lenin introduce the New Economic Policy? [6]
items.answer: (a) Factories and industry were nationalised. Grain was requisitioned from peasants by force. Private trade was banned. Food was rationed, with more for workers and soldiers. Strict discipline was imposed in factories. (b) War Communism had caused economic collapse and famine in 1921. Peasants resisted requisitioning and grew less grain. Workers went on strike and the Kronstadt sailors rebelled. Lenin needed to restore production and win back support.

items.stem: In March 1921 sailors at the Kronstadt naval base rebelled against the Bolsheviks. ‘The Bolsheviks won the Civil War mainly because of the weaknesses of the Whites.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The Whites were divided and had no common aims. Their forces were spread around the edges of Russia. White brutality and links to landlords lost peasant support. Against: Trotsky's leadership created an effective Red Army. The Reds held the central areas, industry and railways. War Communism supplied the army. The Cheka's Red Terror crushed opposition behind the lines. Judgement: White weaknesses were important, but the Reds won because they used their central position and Trotsky's leadership to make the most of them.

items.stem: By 1929 Stalin had defeated his rivals for the leadership of the USSR. (a) Describe how Stalin defeated his rivals between 1924 and 1929. [4] (b) Why was Stalin able to become leader of the USSR by 1929? [6]
items.answer: (a) He used his position as General Secretary to promote supporters. He allied with Zinoviev and Kamenev against Trotsky. Lenin's Testament was not published, which protected him. He then allied with Bukharin against Zinoviev and Kamenev. Trotsky was expelled in 1927 and exiled in 1929, and Bukharin was removed from the Politburo in 1929. (b) As General Secretary he controlled appointments and built a loyal following. His rivals underestimated him as a dull bureaucrat. Trotsky was disliked and seen as arrogant, and failed to build support. Stalin cleverly switched alliances, using rivals against each other. Socialism in One Country was more popular than Permanent Revolution.

items.stem: Describe the purges of the 1930s.
items.answer: After Kirov's murder in 1934 Stalin used the NKVD to arrest suspected enemies. Leading communists such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin confessed at show trials and were executed. The Red Army was purged, including Marshal Tukhachevsky. Ordinary people were denounced, arrested and sent to the gulags. Hundreds of thousands were executed in 1937-38 alone.

items.stem: Study the figures. Official Soviet production figures (million tonnes): Coal: 1928 35.4, 1932 64.4, 1937 128.0. Steel: 1928 4.0, 1932 5.9, 1937 17.7. Oil: 1928 11.7, 1932 21.4, 1937 28.5. Calculate the percentage increase in coal production between 1932 and 1937.

Study the figures. Official Soviet production figures (million tonnes): Coal: 1928 35.4, 1932 64.4, 1937 128.0. Steel: 1928 4.0, 1932 5.9, 1937 17.7. Oil: 1928 11.7, 1932 21.4, 1937 28.5. (a) By how many times did steel production increase between 1928 and 1932? [2] (b) Give two reasons why a historian should treat these figures with caution. [2] (c) Explain how the Five-Year Plans achieved such increases. [4]
items.answer: (a) 5.9 ÷ 4.0 ≈ 1.5 times. (b) They are official figures, and managers had reasons to exaggerate output to meet targets; they show quantity, not quality, and say nothing about the human cost. (c) Resources were concentrated on heavy industry; new plants such as Magnitogorsk were built; workers were driven by targets, propaganda (Stakhanovites) and punishment; gulag labour was used.

items.stem: ‘Stalin's economic policies were a success.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Industrial output grew rapidly: coal production rose from about 35 to 128 million tonnes between 1928 and 1937. New industrial cities, dams and railways were built. The USSR was able to produce the weapons that helped defeat Germany after 1941. Against: Collectivisation caused a famine in which millions died. Grain and livestock production fell. Consumer goods and housing were neglected. Millions of forced labourers suffered and died in the gulags. Judgement: The policies achieved Stalin's aim of rapid industrialisation, but at an enormous human cost, so they were a success only by his own narrow measure.

items.stem: In April 1917 Lenin returned to Russia from exile in Switzerland. How important was Lenin in the Bolshevik seizure of power? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: His April Theses gave the Bolsheviks popular slogans. He insisted on seizing power in October against doubters such as Zinoviev and Kamenev. Against: Trotsky planned and carried out the takeover. The failures of the Provisional Government did much of the work. The Kornilov affair gave the Bolsheviks weapons and credibility. Judgement: Lenin was vital in deciding that the Bolsheviks should take power, but Trotsky's organisation and the government's weakness were essential too.

items.stem: How far was the NEP a success? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Agricultural and industrial production recovered. It ended the famine and the unrest of 1921. It helped the Bolsheviks keep power. Against: Many communists saw it as a betrayal of socialism. Nepmen and richer peasants (kulaks) prospered, increasing inequality. Industry recovered more slowly than farming (the “scissors crisis”). Judgement: The NEP was an economic and political success in the short term, but it divided the party and was abandoned by Stalin in 1928.

items.stem: By 1929 Stalin had defeated his rivals for the leadership of the USSR. Describe how Stalin defeated his rivals between 1924 and 1929.
items.answer: He used his position as General Secretary to promote supporters. He allied with Zinoviev and Kamenev against Trotsky. Lenin's Testament was not published, which protected him. He then allied with Bukharin against Zinoviev and Kamenev. Trotsky was expelled in 1927 and exiled in 1929, and Bukharin was removed from the Politburo in 1929.

items.stem: Describe the Five-Year Plans.
items.answer: Gosplan set production targets for every industry. Heavy industry such as coal, steel, oil and electricity was the priority. New industrial cities such as Magnitogorsk were built. Huge projects such as the Dnieper dam and the Moscow metro were completed. Workers faced harsh discipline, and gulag prisoners provided forced labour.

items.stem: ‘Stalin's economic policies were a success.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Industrial output grew rapidly: coal production rose from about 35 to 128 million tonnes between 1928 and 1937. New industrial cities, dams and railways were built. The USSR was able to produce the weapons that helped defeat Germany after 1941. Against: Collectivisation caused a famine in which millions died. Grain and livestock production fell. Consumer goods and housing were neglected. Millions of forced labourers suffered and died in the gulags. Judgement: The policies achieved Stalin's aim of rapid industrialisation, but at an enormous human cost, so they were a success only by his own narrow measure.

items.stem: Describe the events of the 1905 Revolution.
items.answer: On Bloody Sunday, troops fired on a peaceful procession led by Father Gapon. Strikes spread across Russia and peasants seized land. Sailors mutinied on the battleship Potemkin. The St Petersburg Soviet was set up, with Trotsky as a leader. The Tsar issued the October Manifesto promising a Duma.

items.stem: How far did collectivisation achieve its aims? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The state gained control over peasants and grain supplies. The kulaks were destroyed. Grain was exported to pay for industrial machinery. Against: Grain production fell in the early 1930s. Famine killed millions. Livestock numbers collapsed and took years to recover. Judgement: Collectivisation achieved Stalin's political aims of control, but failed to increase food production.
